title: SIM Card, eSIM, or Pocket WiFi in Korea? A Beginner's Guide to Staying Connected
html:
Before you land in Korea, you'll want a way to get online — for maps, translation apps, messaging your hotel, and calling a taxi. You have three main options: a physical prepaid SIM card, an eSIM (a "virtual" SIM built into your phone), or a pocket WiFi device you carry around. None of them is the single "best" choice — it depends on your phone, your group size, and whether you need an actual Korean phone number. Here's what each one actually involves.

Physical prepaid SIM card

A prepaid SIM card is a small chip you swap into your phone that gives you a real Korean phone number, plus data, calls, and texts. This is the option to pick if you need a Korean number — for example, to receive a text verification code for a Korean app, book a restaurant by phone, or call a taxi company directly.

SIM cards come in a few different sizes (standard, micro, nano) — tell the counter staff your phone model and they'll give you the right one, or cut it down for you on the spot. Photo: Tony Webster, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. Source.

All three Korean carriers — SK Telecom, KT, and LG U+ — sell tourist SIM cards, and prices are all similar: roughly ₩30,000–₩55,000 for about a week of unlimited data plus calls and texts, depending on how many days you need. You'll need to show your passport when you buy one — it's a legal requirement in Korea, not just a formality, so don't leave it in your hotel room on the day you buy your SIM.

What locals actually do: Korean residents sign long-term contracts tied to their resident registration number, so they never touch a tourist SIM counter at all — these counters exist specifically for short-term visitors who can't get a regular Korean phone contract.

eSIM — set it up before you even land

An eSIM does the same job as a physical SIM card, but there's no plastic chip to swap — it's a small digital profile you install on your phone over WiFi, usually by scanning a QR code. Most phones from the last few years support it (check your phone's settings for "eSIM" or search your exact model online if you're not sure).

An eSIM (right) is just a chip built into your phone already — nothing to insert or lose. Diagram: Jbond2018, via Wikimedia Commons, Public Domain (CC0). Source.

Most tourist eSIMs for Korea are data-only — no calls, no texts, and no Korean phone number — which is fine if you mainly need maps and messaging apps like KakaoTalk or WhatsApp. Because there's no number attached, you usually don't even need to show your passport to buy one. Plans typically run around ₩15,000–₩25,000 for about a week, sold online by the carriers themselves or by third-party sites (Klook, Trazy, Airalo, and similar).

  • Buy it a few days before your trip and you'll get an email with a QR code.
  • On iPhone: Settings → Cellular → Add eSIM → Scan QR Code.
  • On Android/Samsung: Settings → Connections → SIM Manager → Add Mobile Plan → scan the QR code with your camera.
  • Install it before you fly, but don't activate it until you land — on most plans, the countdown of days starts the moment you turn it on, so activating early just wastes days.
  • Once it's installed, set it as your data line (not your main line) and make sure data roaming is switched on for it, or you won't get any signal after landing.

If your phone is an older model without eSIM support, or you'd rather have a backup physical card, you can still buy a regular tourist SIM instead — see the section above.

Pocket WiFi (WiFi egg)

A pocket WiFi, often called a "WiFi egg" because of its rounded shape, is a small rechargeable device that creates its own WiFi hotspot. Instead of putting a SIM in your own phone, you connect your phone (and everyone else's) to this one device.

A pocket WiFi device (also called a mobile hotspot or "MiFi") — the exact model you're handed at the airport counter will look different, but they all work the same way. Photo: Fegmenmar, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. Source.

This is the best option for families or groups travelling together, since one device (usually good for up to 3–5 connections) can cover everyone, and it's often cheaper per person than buying separate SIMs. It also works for laptops and tablets, not just phones. Expect to pay around ₩8,000–₩12,000 per day, and you'll need your passport plus a credit card (Visa or Mastercard, under the same name as your passport) to pick one up.

The trade-off: it's one more physical thing to carry and charge every night, everyone in your group has to stay within WiFi range of it, and you'll pay a late fee (commonly around ₩3,300/day) if you forget to return it on time. You can usually return it in a drop box at the airport when you leave, even if you picked it up somewhere else, like Myeongdong or Hongdae.

Picking up your SIM or WiFi at Incheon Airport

If you didn't order online in advance, you can walk up and buy or rent any of the above right after you land.

The arrival hall at Incheon Airport Terminal 1, where the telecom counters are located. Photo: Arne Müseler, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 DE. Source.

  • SK Telecom, KT, and LG U+ all have counters in the arrival halls of both Terminal 1 and Terminal 2 at Incheon Airport — you'll see all three close together. Some counters run 24 hours, others roughly 6am–10pm, so if you're landing very late at night, check ahead or plan to buy a SIM at a convenience store in the city instead.
  • Staff at these counters are used to foreign travelers and speak enough English to help you pick a plan.
  • The same counters handle both SIM cards and pocket WiFi pickup/return.
  • If you're flying into Gimpo (mostly domestic and some Japan/China flights) or Busan's Gimhae Airport instead, smaller versions of the same counters are usually available there too.

Which one should you pick?

Option Starting cost Gives you a Korean number? Best for
Physical SIM card ~₩30,000–55,000 / week Yes Solo travelers who need calls/texts or app verification
eSIM ~₩15,000–25,000 / week No (data only) Anyone with a newer phone who just needs data, and wants it ready before landing
Pocket WiFi ~₩8,000–12,000 / day No Families and groups sharing one device, or anyone bringing a laptop/tablet

Practical tips

  • Make sure your phone is unlocked before you travel — a phone still locked to your home carrier can't use a Korean SIM or eSIM. If you're not sure, ask your home carrier or check your phone's settings before you fly.
  • Your home country's data roaming is usually far more expensive than any of these three options, so it's worth setting one of them up even for a short trip.
  • Download Naver Map or KakaoMap and KakaoTalk before you land if you can, using airport WiFi — then you're ready to go the moment your SIM or eSIM connects.
  • Keep your data plan's end date in mind — unlike T-money balance, unused SIM/eSIM/WiFi days don't roll over or refund if your trip runs short.

💬 Not sure which option fits your trip? Tell us your phone model and group size in the comments and we'll help you figure it out!
